query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A minor modification of the equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr composition by adding a small amount (≈2 at.%) of aluminum will enable the formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 surface scale during high-temperature oxidation, thereby improving its oxygen resistance without compromising its room‐ and high‐temperature mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% tensile ductility at room temperature and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Modify the alloy by adding about 2 atomic percent aluminum while keeping all other elements at equiatomic ratios.
generation.conditions: Expose the alloy (with and without Al addition) to air at 800 °C for 5 hours under no applied load; subsequent mechanical testing (e.g., tensile tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C) to verify that the mechanical properties are preserved.
generation.structural_mediator: The added Al preferentially oxidizes to form a thin, dense, and adherent alumina (Al2O3) layer on the surface.
generation.mechanism: Because Al2O3 is thermodynamically stable and possesses a low oxygen permeability, its formation on the alloy surface serves as a protective diffusion barrier. The protective oxide inhibits further oxygen ingress (and thus pesting) while minimally affecting the bulk microstructure and mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, the Al-modified alloy will experience significantly lower oxidation mass gain and will not exhibit pesting during a 5-hour air exposure at 800 °C, while maintaining its ductility and high-temperature yield strength.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr, which shows inadequate oxygen resistance (e.g., pesting or rapid oxidation) under similar exposure conditions.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies for oxidation conditions around 800 °C in air for exposures on the order of 5 hours, and under zero or negligible external mechanical loading. The effect on the oxidation behavior in different atmospheres or over substantially longer exposures remains uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The precise optimal Al content and its impact on long‐term phase stability or any minor modifications in room‐temperature ductility have not been fully determined. Additionally, interactions with processing parameters may further modify the effectiveness of the protective scale.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples using identical casting routes: one set of baseline equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr and another set with a 2 at.% Al addition. After ensuring similar microstructures and mechanical properties in the as-cast state, expose both sample sets to air at 800 °C for 5 hours without applied stress. After exposure, assess oxidation by measuring mass gain per surface area, examine oxide scale morphology and adhesion (using SEM/EDS), and perform tensile tests at room temperature and 1000 °C.
measurements: Quality (continuity, adherence) of the oxide scale via microscopy
Retention of room-temperature ductility (8–16%) and high-temperature yield strength (163–530 MPa)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-modified alloy does not exhibit a significantly lower mass gain and a more coherent (protective) oxide scale when compared to the untreated alloy – or if the mechanical properties degrade beyond acceptable limits – then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Concurrent strength–ductility improvement of HfMoTaTiZr is achieved via Cr addition and the underlying strengthening mechanism was discussed. 4.2 at% Cr addition into HfMoTaTiZr led to the formation of a Laves phase, in addition to the BCC phase. The hardness of HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 is 535.8 Hv 0.3 , 56.96% higher than the reference alloy HfMoTaTiZr. The yield strength and fracture strain of HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 reach 1750.6 ± 80.3 MPa and 14.0 ± 2.9%, respectively, 207.5 MPa and 20.6% higher than HfMoTaTiZr. Solid solution hardening and the presence of the intermetallic Laves phase are believed to be responsible for the enhancement in strength and the formation of a reticulated structure of the Laves phase in HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 results in the improvement in ductility.

Recently the concept of high-entropy alloys (HEAs), consisting of four or more principle metallic elements in equiatomic or near-equiatomic ratios, has attracted considerable interest owing to its tendency to form solid solution with outstanding mechanical and functional properties [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] , [6] ]. By introducing refractory elements including group IV (Ti, Zr, and Hf), V (V, Nb, and Ta), and VI (Cr, Mo, and W) in HEAs, the developed refractory HEAs (RHEAs) possess high melting temperature, outstanding strength and hardness, high thermal stability, and softening resistance at elevated temperatures, which opens up the possibilities of the alloy developments satisfying structural demands at high temperature.

Since the first WMoTaNb RHEA was reported in 2010, many literatures have been focused on the preparation methods and mechanical properties of RHEAs [ [7] , [8] ]. For example, the BCC WMoTaNb and WMoTaNbV HEAs maintained yield strength of 405 and 477 MPa at 1600 °C respectively, which were much higher than that of Inconel 718 and Haynes 230 [ [9] ].
